fields.title: Why the Model Makes Things Up
fields.keyTakeaway: A hallucination is a consequence of how the model is built, not a defect, and is reduced by grounding, the right to refuse, and the requirement for a quote, while exact data must be shown by the product rather than generated.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Where do confident incorrect answers come from, and can they be eliminated?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: A [[hallucination|hallucination]] is not a bug, but a consequence of how the model is built: it predicts a plausible continuation rather than checking for truth. Expecting the model to "learn not to lie" leads to a lack of protection.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: The model generates what is plausible. If data is missing, it still generates something plausible, which is where confident fabrications come from.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: What reduces the frequency, in order of effectiveness:
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: **[[grounding|Grounding]].** Providing data in the context and requiring answers based solely on it. This is the main technique, and it is RAG.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **The right to say "I don't know".** The prompt must explicitly allow and encourage refusal. Without this, the model is forced to answer something and will make things up.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: **Requirement for a quote.** The answer must contain a snippet of the source. This sharply reduces fabrications: it is harder to quote something that does not exist.
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: **Post-generation validation.** Programmatic or via a separate call: check whether the statement is contained in the context. This is expensive and applied to critical scenarios.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: **Low temperature.** It helps a little and does not solve the problem.
fields.sections/2/blocks/7/text: What does **not** work: asking "do not make things up" without grounding; a stronger model by itself; increasing the context length.
fields.sections/2/blocks/8/text: Separately — **recognizing where a hallucination is dangerous.** A made-up phrasing in a description is minor. A made-up product ingredient is a health hazard. The level of protection matches the cost of failure, not a general pursuit of quality.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: Classification of scenarios by cost of failure:
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/rows/0/2: Quote from description only, otherwise refusal
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/rows/1/2: Not through the model at all, direct data
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: Second, an important product decision: **price and availability do not pass through the model at all.** They are injected into the interface as data. The model can mention an item, but the number next to it is not its own.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: This is a general rule: **exact data is shown by the product, not generated.**
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: The refusal rule in the prompt is strict: if the information is not in the provided description, the answer is "not specified in the description" plus a link. Evals check this with a separate criterion and a 98% threshold.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Hallucinations cannot be completely eliminated. The goal is to make them rare and harmless, not zero.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: A hallucination is a consequence of how the model is built, not a defect, and is reduced by grounding, the right to refuse, and the requirement for a quote, while exact data must be shown by the product rather than generated.
